metadata.title: Cisco Stock's Independent Streak Is Its Edge

content.text:
The stock's recent pop is grabbing attention, but its real value lies in how it moves differently from the market you already own.
Cisco Systems (CSCO) has been on a tear, jumping 4.7% in the last 5 trading days while the broader S&P 500 barely moved, up just 0.5%. This comes in the context of a business that, on its last earnings call, reported record revenue and a surge in demand for its AI infrastructure.
When a well-known tech name breaks out like this, the instinct is simple: greed. It's the fear of missing out, the urge to jump on a moving train before it leaves the station for good.
But the question that actually builds your wealth isn't whether you can catch next week's momentum. It's about what owning this stock does to your entire portfolio's risk. How much of Cisco's performance is its own unique story, and how much is just a reflection of the market you likely already hold in an index fund?
A Differentiated Return Engine
Over the long run, Cisco's performance is distinct from the market tide. Its 5-year correlation to the S&P 500 is 0.58, a moderate figure that tells you it shares some of the market's general direction but keeps a substantial amount of its behavior to itself. For an investor seeking growth, that combination is attractive: you're getting a return stream that offers genuine diversification from the index.
And the returns have been strong. Over the past 5 years, Cisco has delivered an annualized return of 20%, outpacing the S&P 500's 13.1%. On a risk-adjusted basis, its Sharpe ratio of 0.72 also comes in ahead of the market's 0.59. But here's what that behavior feels like in your portfolio: over the past year, on days the S&P 500 climbed, Cisco captured about 143% of the market's gain. On days the market fell, it absorbed only about 98% of the loss. It has historically amplified the upside while slightly softening the downside.
AI Fuel, Margin Questions
That independent performance is grounded in a business undergoing a significant shift. The excitement is clearly centered on artificial intelligence. On its latest call, management announced it now expects to take "AI infrastructure orders of approximately $9 billion from hyperscalers in FY '26," which is 4.5x its FY '25 total. This rapid demand for its networking gear, powered by its proprietary Silicon One technology and Acacia Optics, is the engine driving the stock's story.
This rapid shift toward hardware, however, has come at a cost to profitability, as the company's non-GAAP product gross margin was down 330 basis points year-over-year in the last quarter. Alongside the AI boom, the company's other segments are also showing strength. Product orders excluding the hyperscalers grew a strong 19%, though some analysts question if that reflects customers pulling orders forward amid supply chain concerns. For more on the company's growth drivers, see what might be the overlooked growth engine powering Cisco Systems stock.
